title: From a Naivasha Campsite to Shipton's Camp: Choosing Sleeping Bags in Nairobi
meta_title: Sleeping Bags in Nairobi: Affordable Warmth for 4 Camp Types
meta_description: Sleeping bags in Nairobi for Kenyan camps: the Comfort rating for Naivasha, the Aberdares and Mt Kenya, down vs synthetic, and what to check on thrifted bags.
excerpt: How to choose sleeping bags in Nairobi by the coldest camp on your trip, from +10°C Rift Valley nights to sub-zero Mt Kenya camps, with down vs synthetic, thrifted checks and where to try one on Thika Road.
content:
A clear night at Shipton's Camp on Mt Kenya can drop below -10°C while Naivasha rarely nears freezing, so buy sleeping bags in Nairobi for the coldest camp you have planned. Pick a Comfort rating a few degrees below that low: about +10°C for the Rift Valley, 0°C for the Aberdares, -5°C or colder for Mt Kenya.

Too thin a bag means lying awake at 3:00am; too heavy means hauling an expedition sack to a lakeside site. Below: how Kenyan camps compare at night, how to read a label, down versus synthetic, thrifted checks, and where to see sleeping bags in Nairobi in person.

Quick Facts

  • Number to buy by: the Comfort rating from the ISO 23537 test (formerly EN 13537)
  • Rift Valley camps (about 1,900-2,100 m): a Comfort rating near +10°C
  • Aberdares and other camps above 3,000 m: a Comfort rating near 0°C
  • Mt Kenya (Old Moses 3,300 m, Shipton's 4,200 m): -5°C or colder
  • Short rains: above-average October-December rain forecast for most of Kenya
  • Where to buy sleeping bags in Nairobi: Mountain Mall, 3rd Floor, Shop D39, Thika Road, or online with M-Pesa or cash on delivery

How Cold Do Kenyan Campsites Get at Night?

Kenyan campsites get colder with height far more than with the month, which is why sleeping bags in Nairobi range from summer bags to mountain bags. Rift Valley lake sites stay mild, highland moorland can touch freezing, and Mt Kenya's high camps sit well below zero on clear nights.

Air cools by roughly 6.5°C per 1,000 m of climb. Nairobi sits at about 1,795 m, so a 4,200 m camp starts about 15°C colder, and a cloudless sky lets heat escape fast. Use this table to match sleeping bags in Nairobi shops to your camp.

Which Temperature Rating Should You Trust?

Trust the Comfort rating. Under ISO 23537 it is the lowest temperature at which a standard woman sleeps comfortably lying relaxed; lower figures assume a warmer sleeper curled up.

  1. Comfort: a relaxed sleeper who feels the cold stays comfortable. Buy by this.
  2. Lower limit: a standard man sleeps about eight hours curled up. Warm sleepers can use it.
  3. Extreme: a survival figure with a real risk of hypothermia. Never plan around it.

What if the label shows only one number?

A single big figure on budget sleeping bags in Nairobi is usually closer to the Limit or Extreme rating than to Comfort. Treat a "-5°C" bag with no breakdown as a 0°C to +5°C bag. Lab tests use a rested manikin, so if you sleep cold, take another 3-5°C off the expected low.

Down or Synthetic for Kenya's Wet Months?

Among sleeping bags in Nairobi, down gives the most warmth for its weight and packs smallest, so it suits Mt Kenya and long carries. Synthetic copes better with damp and costs less, so it suits rainy-season camps and first bags.

The Kenya Meteorological Department expected above-average short rains over about 80% of Kenya, with Nairobi's rains running from mid-October into January, in its October-December seasonal forecast. A dripping tent punishes down far more than polyester, so synthetic fill makes sense for camping before January.

Mummy, rectangular or in between?

A mummy bag tapers and has a hood, leaving less air to heat; take one above 3,000 m. Rectangular sleeping bags in Nairobi are cheaper and roomier, and many unzip into a duvet. Our post on a 15°C mummy-shape down sleeping bag shows a light, warm-weather mummy for lowland camps.

What to Check When Buying Sleeping Bags in Nairobi

Check five things before you pay: Comfort rating, fill, length, zip and loft. A bag that fits, closes fully and springs back after squashing will last.

How long should the bag be?

Lie in it. Leave a hand's width beyond your feet for a water bottle or socks, but no more, because empty space is cold space. Regular lengths suit people up to about 180 cm; taller campers need a long size.

Are thrifted sleeping bags in Nairobi worth it?

Often, yes: a branded down bag stored loose can keep its loft for a decade. The sleeping bags in Nairobi that we stock are mostly quality thrifted, plus some new, which puts a warm, well-known bag within reach for far less than new. Our thrifted outdoor gear post covers pre-owned buying. Check any used bag yourself:

Is the sleeping mat as important as the bag?

Yes. Your weight crushes the insulation beneath you, so the ground steals heat unless a mat stops it. Sea to Summit, which makes liners and mats, says no liner can make up for an inadequate pad. Above 3,000 m, use an insulated mat with a higher R-value. Shoppers comparing sleeping bags in Nairobi often forget this half of the system.

Pro Tips: A Warmer Night in Camp

  • Change before bed: swap damp hiking clothes for dry thermals and socks
  • Close the hood: pull the drawcord until only your face shows
  • Add a liner: Sea to Summit estimates its fleece liner adds up to 8°C, as a rough guide
  • Keep it dry: pack the bag in a dry bag or bin liner
  • Store it loose: at home, hang it or keep it in a big cotton sack

Two Worked Examples: Naivasha and Mt Kenya

Warm sleep comes from four things matched to the camp: bag, mat, clothes and hat.

A weekend at a Naivasha campsite

The lighter sleeping bags in Nairobi shops, rated near +10°C, are plenty here, on a 1-2 cm foam mat. Sleep in a long-sleeve top with a fleece nearby for the small hours. In the short rains, synthetic is the safer fill, and a waterproof rechargeable headlamp helps in a wet tent. Our camping gear in Nairobi post covers tents and stoves.

Four nights on Mt Kenya's Sirimon route

For Old Moses and Shipton's (see our Mt Kenya hiking guide), take a down mummy rated -5°C or colder, an insulated mat, thermals and dry merino wool hiking socks for sleeping. A fleece-lined balaclava stops heat leaking when the hood shifts. Our thermal wear post covers base layers, and the hiking gear checklist for Kenya has the full packing list.

Common Mistakes on a First Night Out

Most cold nights come from a few habits, and no upgrade among sleeping bags in Nairobi fixes them.

  • Sleeping in sweat-damp hiking clothes instead of dry layers.
  • Skipping the mat, or using a yoga mat on frozen ground.
  • Getting in cold. The bag holds heat but does not make it, so move briskly first.
  • Leaving the hood open on a -5°C night.
  • Packing the bag away damp after the trip, which invites mildew.

How Do You Care for a Sleeping Bag Between Trips?

Dry it fully after every trip, store it loose, and wash it only when dirty. Care protects the loft, and loft keeps you warm.

Months in a compression sack crush the fill for good, so hang the bag or use a large breathable sack. A liner keeps skin oils off the inside. When you do wash, use a down-specific or synthetic-safe wash and dry slowly, breaking up clumps by hand. Good storage is the cheapest way to make sleeping bags in Nairobi last.

Before camping in a park or forest reserve, confirm rules and current fees with the Kenya Wildlife Service or the Kenya Forest Service. For cooking, our camping gas in Nairobi post matches cartridges to stoves.

Frequently Asked Questions

What temperature sleeping bag do I need for Mt Kenya?

Mt Kenya calls for a sleeping bag with a Comfort rating of about -5°C or colder, because Shipton's and Mackinder's camps sit around 4,200 m and clear nights can fall below -10°C. A hooded mummy with a neck collar holds heat best. Pair it with an insulated mat, and when shopping for sleeping bags in Nairobi for this climb, ask for the Comfort figure.

Can I find a cheap sleeping bag that is still warm?

Yes, and thrifted is the easiest route, because branded bags from good outdoor makers last for years when stored loose. Check that the loft springs back and the zip runs the full length. A pre-owned down bag usually costs far less than the same bag new; ask for its Comfort rating.

Is down or synthetic better for camping in Kenya?

Down is better for Kenyan treks where weight and pack space matter, such as Mt Kenya and Kilimanjaro, if you keep it dry. Synthetic is better for rainy-season camping, damp lakeside sites and tighter budgets, because it holds more warmth when wet and dries faster. Many campers buying sleeping bags in Nairobi end up owning both.

Do I need a sleeping bag at Lake Naivasha?

Camping at Lake Naivasha usually needs a light sleeping bag with a Comfort rating around +10°C, since Rift Valley nights turn cool after midnight but seldom freeze. In the October-December rains, choose synthetic fill or keep a down bag sealed in a dry bag.

How long does a sleeping bag last?

A down sleeping bag can last ten years or more if it is dried after trips, stored loose and washed only when dirty. A synthetic bag usually loses warmth within a few years of regular use, because its fibres flatten with each compression. A liner and loose storage add years to both.

Final Thoughts

Choose sleeping bags in Nairobi for the coldest night on your plan, read the Comfort figure rather than the headline number, and give the mat as much thought as the bag. Down rewards trekkers who keep it dry; synthetic forgives wet tents and tight budgets.
